nl:
**System Overview**

The model describes a very simple marketplace for a fixed set of *credits* that can be owned by a fixed set of *businesses*.  
At any moment the system keeps two pieces of state:

1. **Ownership map** – for each credit the model records which business currently holds it.  
2. **Pending offers** – a collection of proposals that have been made but not yet acted upon. Each proposal records three items: the business that is offering the credit (the *seller*), the business that is being asked to receive the credit (the *buyer*), and the credit itself.

The system starts with an arbitrary initial distribution of the credits among the businesses, and with no pending proposals.

---

**Actions**

The behaviour of the marketplace is captured by three possible actions that can be performed on a single credit at a time. All actions involve two distinct businesses, a *from* business and a *to* business, and a specific credit.

| Action | When it can occur | Effect on the state |
|--------|-------------------|---------------------|
| **Propose** | The *from* business must already own the credit. | A new proposal `<from, to, credit>` is added to the set of pending offers. Ownership does **not** change. |
| **Accept** | There must already be a pending proposal `<from, to, credit>`. | The proposal is removed from the pending set, and ownership of the credit is transferred from *from* to *to*. |
| **Reject** | There must already be a pending proposal `<from, to, credit>`. | The proposal is simply removed; ownership stays with the original owner. |

In addition to these three logical actions, the model allows a *no‑op* step that prints the current state (used only for debugging). This step does not modify any variable.

The model’s “Next” step says that in each transition the system nondeterministically picks any two different businesses and any credit, and then performs **one** of the four possibilities above (Propose, Accept, Reject, or the debug print). Thus the system can interleave proposals, acceptances, and rejections in any order.

---

**Safety Requirement (Invariant)**

The model includes a global safety rule called **ChangeInvariant**. It states that whenever the ownership of a particular credit changes from one business to another, that change must be the direct result of an **Accept** action that matches a previously existing proposal. In other words, a credit may only be transferred if:

1. The former owner had previously made a proposal offering that credit to the new owner, **and**  
2. The new owner subsequently performed an Accept step for that exact proposal.

No other pathway (e.g., a spontaneous reassignment, a reject, or a proposal without acceptance) is allowed to alter the owner of a credit.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
A credit can change its owner only by an explicit acceptance of a pending offer that was originally made by the current owner to the new owner; any ownership change must be preceded by a matching proposal and must be performed by the Accept action.

**System Overview** The model describes a simple storage service that supports two kinds of client requests – writes that store a user’s metadata together with an image, and reads that retrieve the latest stored metadata and image for a user. The service is composed of a set of *servers* that handle the client requests and a set of *cleaner* processes that periodically delete image blobs that are no longer referenced by any user record. All state is kept in two stores: * a **database** that maps each user identifier to a pair *(metadata, image‑id)*, and * a **blob store** that maps each globally‑unique identifier (UUID) to the actual image data. Both stores start empty (all entries contain the special value **UNSET**) and evolve as the servers and cleaners perform actions. --- ### Variables and What They Represent | Variable | Meaning | |----------|---------| | **database_state** | A map from every user id to a record containing the user’s current metadata value and a reference (UUID) to the image stored for that user. If a user has never been written, both fields are **UNSET**. | | **blob_store_state** | A map from every UUID to the image data stored under that identifier. An entry that is **UNSET** means the UUID does not correspond to a stored image. | | **server_state** | For each server, a record describing what the server is doing at the moment. The record contains:
• *state* – one of **waiting**, **started_write**, **wrote_blob**, **started_read**, **read_metadata**;
• *user_id* – the user that the current request concerns (or **UNSET**);
• *metadata* – the metadata value being written or read (or **UNSET**);
• *image_id* – the UUID of the image being written or read (or **UNSET**);
• *image* – the actual image value being written (or **UNSET**). | | **cleaner_state** | For each cleaner, a record that tracks its progress through a cleaning cycle. The record contains:
• *state* – one of **waiting**, **got_blob_keys**, **got_unused_keys**, **deleting_keys**;
• *blob_keys* – the set of all UUIDs that currently have an image stored in the blob store;
• *unused_blob_keys* – the subset of *blob_keys* that are not referenced by any user record in the database. | | **operations** | A chronological list (log) of all client operations that have been observed by the model. Each entry records the operation type (**READ** or **WRITE**) together with the user id, metadata value and image value that were returned (or **UNSET** for reads that found nothing). | All variables are constrained to contain only values drawn from the predefined constant sets (user ids, metadata versions, image versions, UUIDs) together with the special **UNSET** placeholder. --- ### Server Actions 1. **StartWrite** – When a server is idle (**waiting**), it nondeterministically picks a user, a metadata value, and an image value, records them in its local state, changes its state to **started_write**, and appends a **WRITE** entry to the operations log (the entry records the chosen user, metadata and image). No store is modified yet. 2. **WriteBlob** – While in **started_write**, the server chooses a fresh UUID that is currently unused in the blob store, stores the selected image under that UUID, records the UUID as *image_id* in its local state, and moves to **wrote_blob**. The database and cleaner state remain unchanged. 3. **WriteMetadataAndReturn** – When the server has stored the blob (**wrote_blob**), it writes the selected metadata and the newly‑created UUID into the database entry for the chosen user, then resets its local record to the idle **waiting** state (clearing all fields). The blob store and cleaner state are untouched. 4. **FailWrite** – A server that is in the middle of a write (either **started_write** or **wrote_blob**) may abort the operation. It simply returns to the idle **waiting** state, discarding any partially filled fields. No store is altered. 5. **StartRead** – An idle server (**waiting**) may receive a read request for any user. It records the user id, switches to **started_read**, and leaves the rest of its state unchanged. 6. **ReadMetadata** – While in **started_read**, if the database already contains a non‑**UNSET** metadata value for the requested user, the server copies that metadata and the associated image‑id into its local record and advances to **read_metadata**. No store is changed. 7. **ReadMetadataAndReturnEmpty** – While in **started_read**, if the database entry for the requested user still contains **UNSET** metadata, the server treats the request as a miss, returns **UNSET** for both metadata and image, appends a **READ** entry with those **UNSET** values to the operations log, and goes back to **waiting**. 8. **ReadBlobAndReturn** – After having successfully read the metadata (**read_metadata**), the server looks up the image data in the blob store using the stored *image_id*, appends a **READ** entry containing the retrieved metadata and image to the operations log, and finally returns to the idle **waiting** state. --- ### Cleaner Actions 1. **CleanerStartGetBlobKeys** – An idle cleaner (**waiting**) collects the current set of all UUIDs that have a stored image (i.e., all keys whose blob‑store entry is not **UNSET**) and stores that set in *blob_keys*. Its state becomes **got_blob_keys**. 2. **CleanerGetUnusedKeys** – From the **got_blob_keys** state, the cleaner computes the subset of those UUIDs that are *not* referenced by any user record in the database (i.e., for every user, the stored *image_id* differs from the UUID). This subset is stored in *unused_blob_keys* and the cleaner moves to **got_unused_keys**. 3. **CleanerDeletingKeys** – As long as *unused_blob_keys* is non‑empty, the cleaner repeatedly picks one UUID from the set, deletes the corresponding image from the blob store (sets the entry back to **UNSET**), and removes the UUID from *unused_blob_keys*. The cleaner stays in **deleting_keys** (or **got_unused_keys** if it has not yet begun deletions). 4. **CleanerFinished** – When *unused_blob_keys* becomes empty, the cleaner resets all of its fields to empty sets and returns to the idle **waiting** state. 5. **CleanerFail** – From any active state (**got_blob_keys**, **got_unused_keys**, **deleting_keys**), the cleaner may fail. It discards any partial progress and returns to **waiting** with empty key sets. No store is altered. --- ### Operations Log The **operations** sequence is only appended to; it never loses entries. It records every client‑visible write (with the exact data that was attempted) and every read (with the data that was returned, or **UNSET** when the database held no entry). The log is used by the safety invariant to reason about consistency. --- ### Safety Invariants 1. **Type Correctness (TypeOk)** – At all times each component of the system holds a value that belongs to its declared domain. For example, every entry in the database contains a metadata value drawn from the allowed metadata set (or **UNSET**), every UUID in the blob store maps to a valid image version (or **UNSET**), and each server and cleaner record only uses the states listed above. This invariant guarantees that the model never reaches an illegal configuration such as a server holding a non‑existent user id or a blob store containing an image that is not part of the defined image set. 2. **Consistent Reads (ConsistentReads)** – For every read recorded in the **operations** log, one of two conditions must hold: * either the read returned **UNSET** for both metadata and image (meaning the database had no entry for that user at the time), or * there exists a prior **WRITE** entry in the log for the same user whose metadata, image, and image‑id exactly match those returned by the read. In other words, a read can never observe a combination of metadata and image that has never been written for that user. Together these invariants form the system’s safety guarantee: the state always respects the declared types, and any information observed by a client through a read operation is either the explicit “no data” result or a faithful snapshot of a previously committed write. --- **SAFETY PROPERTY:** The system never reaches a state where a value stored outside its declared domain appears, and every read operation observed in the log either returns the special “unset” result (indicating no prior write for that user) or returns exactly the metadata and image that were written earlier for that same user.

**System Overview**

The model describes a simple water‑handling device that consists of two containers (jugs):

* **Big jug** – can hold up to 5 liters of water. The variable *big* records how many liters are currently in this jug.
* **Small jug** – can hold up to 3 liters of water. The variable *small* records how many liters are currently in this jug.

Both variables are always non‑negative integers and never exceed the physical capacities of their respective jugs.

**Initial State**

At the start of execution both jugs are empty; that is, the big jug contains 0 L and the small jug contains 0 L.

**Possible Actions**

From any reachable state the system may perform one of the following six actions:

1. **Fill the small jug** – the small jug is filled to its maximum capacity (3 L); the amount in the big jug does not change.
2. **Fill the big jug** – the big jug is filled to its maximum capacity (5 L); the amount in the small jug does not change.
3. **Empty the small jug** – all water is poured out of the small jug, leaving it with 0 L; the big jug is unchanged.
4. **Empty the big jug** – all water is poured out of the big jug, leaving it with 0 L; the small jug is unchanged.
5. **Pour from small to big** – water is transferred from the small jug into the big jug. The transfer continues until either the big jug becomes full (5 L) or the small jug becomes empty, whichever happens first. After the pour, the big jug’s level is increased by the amount transferred and the small jug’s level is decreased by the same amount.
6. **Pour from big to small** – water is transferred from the big jug into the small jug. The transfer continues until either the small jug becomes full (3 L) or the big jug becomes empty, whichever happens first. After the pour, the big jug’s level is decreased by the amount transferred and the small jug’s level is increased by the same amount.

These actions may be taken in any order, repeatedly, as long as the resulting water levels remain within the physical limits of the two jugs.

**Safety Guarantees (Invariants)**

Two properties are enforced throughout all executions:

* **Range safety** – the amount of water in each jug never leaves its allowed range (0 L to 5 L for the big jug, 0 L to 3 L for the small jug). This guarantees that no action can create an illegal state such as a negative amount of water or a level exceeding a jug’s capacity.
* **No four‑liter state** – the big jug is never allowed to contain exactly 4 L of water. The system’s actions and the initial condition together ensure that this particular volume can never be reached.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The big jug never holds exactly four liters of water.

**System Overview** The specification models a simple distributed counter that is updated by a fixed set of nodes. Each node repeatedly receives a “delta” (an integer between 1 and 3) that it is supposed to add to a globally shared integer stored under the key *counter* in a key‑value store. The global store is accessed atomically with a compare‑and‑swap operation, guaranteeing that only one node can successfully apply its delta when the store still contains the value the node observed earlier. **State Variables** | Variable | Meaning | |----------|---------| | **messages** (`msgs`) | The complete list of messages that will ever be sent. Each message includes the identifier of the destination node and the amount (`delta`) that the node must add to the counter. | | **received** (`recv`) | The subset of `messages` that have already been applied to the counter. It starts empty and grows until it eventually contains every message. | | **node state** (`nodes`) | For every node the specification keeps three pieces of data:
• `current` – the value of the global counter that the node observed when it last fetched a message.
• `msg` – the particular message that the node is currently trying to apply (or a placeholder before a message is selected).
• `pc` – a program‑counter that indicates what the node is ready to do next; it can be either **Add** (looking for a new message) or **Update** (trying to apply the previously fetched message). | | **key‑value store** (`kv`) | A simple sequentially consistent map that contains a single entry: the key *counter* whose value is the current total of all applied deltas. The store starts at 0. | **Operations (informal description)** *Receiving a message* – When a node decides to apply a message, the message is added to `received`. This records globally that the delta has been accounted for. *Reading the counter* – Any node can look up the current value of *counter* in the key‑value store; this operation returns an integer. *Compare‑and‑swap (CAS)* – Before a node can increase the counter, it checks whether the store still holds the exact value it saw earlier (`current`). If the check succeeds, the node atomically writes a new value equal to `current + delta`. If the check fails, the node leaves the store unchanged and will try again later. **Node Actions** 1. **Add (node selects a message)** *Precondition*: The node’s program‑counter is **Add**. *Effect*: The node picks any message whose destination matches the node and that has not yet been recorded in `received`. It stores that message locally, records the current value of the global counter in its `current` field, and switches its program‑counter to **Update**. No other part of the state changes. 2. **Update (node tries to apply its delta)** *Precondition*: The node’s program‑counter is **Update**. *Effect*: The node performs a CAS on the global counter using the `current` value it saved earlier. *If the CAS succeeds* – the counter is increased by the message’s delta, the message is added to `received`, and the node’s program‑counter is reset to **Add**. *If the CAS fails* – the store and `received` stay unchanged, but the node still resets its program‑counter to **Add** so that it will select a (possibly different) message on the next round. The set of messages (`msgs`) never changes. 3. **Termination** (a bookkeeping step) – When every message in `msgs` has been recorded in `received`, the system may stop making further changes; this represents a quiescent state where all work is finished. **Execution Model** The system starts with all nodes in the **Add** state, no messages received, and the counter at 0. At each step any node may execute either its **Add** or **Update** action, subject to its current program‑counter. The specification requires *weak fairness*: each node will infinitely often be given the chance to perform both actions, so no node can be permanently starved. **Derived Quantities** The model defines a way to compute the sum of the `delta` fields of any set of messages. In particular, it can compute the total of all messages that have been received (`recv`) and the total of all messages that exist (`msgs`). These sums are used in the invariant and the liveness property. **Safety Property (Invariant)** The invariant, named **EveryNodeReturnsLatestValue**, asserts that at any reachable state the value read by any node from the global counter equals the sum of the deltas of *all* messages that have already been recorded as received. In other words, every node’s view of the counter is always exactly the total of the increments that have successfully been applied so far; no node ever sees a stale or over‑inflated value. **SAFETY PROPERTY:** Every node, when it reads the shared counter, always obtains a value that is precisely the sum of the deltas of all messages that have been recorded as received up to that moment. This guarantees that the counter never diverges from the total of applied increments.

**System Overview** The model describes a small distributed system that coordinates exclusive access to a shared resource (the *critical section*) among a fixed number of processes. The number of processes is a constant supplied when the model is instantiated (in the accompanying configuration it is set to 2, but any positive integer may be used). --- ### State Variables | Variable | Meaning | |----------|---------| | **processes** | A table that stores, for each process, the current phase of that process in the lock protocol. The possible phases are:
  *AcquireLock* – the process is about to request the lock.
  *WaitForLock* – the process has placed its request in the queue and is waiting for its turn.
  *EnterCriticalSection* – the process has been granted the lock and is now executing the critical section.
  *LeaveCriticalSection* – the process is finishing the critical section and will release the lock. | | **lock** | A FIFO queue (implemented as a sequence) that records the order in which processes have asked for the lock. The first element of the queue is the process that currently holds the lock; the remaining elements are waiting processes. When the queue is empty the lock is free. | Initially every process is in the *AcquireLock* phase and the lock queue is empty. --- ### Actions (Protocol Steps) Each process repeatedly performs the following four actions, depending on its current phase. 1. **AcquireLock (self)** *Pre‑condition*: the process `self` is in the *AcquireLock* phase. *Effect*: `self` appends its identifier to the end of the lock queue, thereby registering a request for the lock. Afterwards it moves to the *WaitForLock* phase. The queue grows by one element; no other part of the state changes. 2. **WaitForLock (self)** *Pre‑condition*: the process `self` is in the *WaitForLock* phase **and** it is at the head of the lock queue (i.e., it is the first element). *Effect*: `self` transitions to the *EnterCriticalSection* phase. The lock queue is left unchanged; only the process’s phase is updated. 3. **EnterCriticalSection (self)** *Pre‑condition*: the process `self` is in the *EnterCriticalSection* phase. *Effect*: `self` moves to the *LeaveCriticalSection* phase. The lock queue stays unchanged; this step represents the execution of the critical section itself. 4. **LeaveCriticalSection (self)** *Pre‑condition*: the process `self` is in the *LeaveCriticalSection* phase. *Effect*: `self` removes the first element from the lock queue (which must be its own identifier), thereby releasing the lock. After that it returns to the *AcquireLock* phase, ready to request the lock again. The system’s overall transition relation allows *any* process whose pre‑condition for one of the four actions holds to take that action. This nondeterministic choice models asynchronous execution where processes can be scheduled in any order. --- ### Fairness Assumptions For each process, every one of the four actions is assumed to be **weakly fair**: if an action becomes continuously enabled for a particular process, the model guarantees that the action will eventually be taken. This prevents a process from being permanently stuck in a state while its request remains enabled. --- ### Intended Behaviour The protocol implements a *first‑come‑first‑served* lock: * When a process wants the lock it records its request at the tail of the queue. * The process at the head of the queue is the only one allowed to enter the critical section. * After finishing, the process removes itself from the head, exposing the next waiting process (if any). Because the queue preserves the order of arrivals and only the head may progress to the critical section, the system gives each process a fair chance to acquire the lock without starvation (under the fairness assumptions). --- ### Safety Property (Invariant) The invariant named **MutualExclusion** asserts that no two distinct processes can be in the *EnterCriticalSection* phase at the same time. In other words, the critical section is never occupied by more than one process. **SAFETY PROPERTY:** At any moment, at most one process may be in the critical section; no two different processes are simultaneously in the “EnterCriticalSection” state.

**System Overview**

The model describes a very small message‑exchange system consisting of a fixed number of client processes (the constant *NumClients*). Each client participates in a simple two‑step protocol:

1. **Send a message** – the client creates a message and places it into a shared pool.
2. **Receive the message** – a receiver (conceptually the system itself) removes a message from the pool and records that it has been processed.

The whole system runs until every client has finished sending its message, after which the system can stop.

---

### State Variables  

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **msgs** | A set that holds the messages that have been sent but not yet processed. Each element of the set is simply the identifier of the client that created the message. |
| **clients** | A map from each client identifier to a record that stores the client’s current state. The state can be either **“SendMessage”** (the client still has to send its message) or **“Done”** (the client has already sent its message). |
| **received** | An ordered list (a sequence) that records, in the order they were taken from *msgs*, every message that has been processed. The list grows one entry each time a message is received. |

At the start of execution the message pool is empty, every client’s state is “SendMessage”, and the *received* list is empty.

---

### Actions  

1. **SendMessage**  
   *When it can happen*: Any client whose state is “SendMessage”.  
   *Effect*:  
   - The client’s identifier is added to the *msgs* set, representing the creation of a new message.  
   - The client’s state is changed to “Done”, indicating that it will not send another message.  
   - The *received* list is left unchanged.  

   In effect, each client sends exactly one message and then becomes inactive.

2. **Receive**  
   *When it can happen*: Whenever there is at least one message in the *msgs* set.  
   *Effect*:  
   - One message *m* is chosen nondeterministically from the set.  
   - That message is removed from *msgs* so it cannot be received again.  
   - The message identifier *m* is appended to the end of the *received* list, recording that the message has been processed.  
   - The client map is unchanged (the clients do not react to the receipt of a message).  

   This action models the system’s processing of a pending message.

3. **Terminating**  
   *When it can happen*: Only when every client’s state is “Done” (i.e., all clients have already sent their messages).  
   *Effect*: No state variables are changed; the system may simply stop. In the original TLA+ model a diagnostic print of the *received* list is performed, but this has no impact on the logical behavior.  

   This action represents the normal shutdown of the system after all work is done.

The overall behavior of the system is any interleaving of the three actions that respects their enabling conditions. The model checker explores all possible orders in which clients may send and the system may receive messages.

---

### Safety Property (Invariant)

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
Every message that appears in the *received* list is unique; no message identifier occurs more than once in the list. In other words, once a message has been taken from the pool and recorded as processed, it can never be processed again. This guarantees that each client’s single message is handled at most one time, preventing duplicate processing.

**System Overview**

The model describes a very small concurrent system that consists of a fixed set of worker threads (the constant *Threads*). In the concrete configuration supplied to the model‑checker there are exactly two threads, called *t1* and *t2*. The system maintains two pieces of shared state:

1. **Per‑thread state** – for every thread the model stores a record with two fields:  
   * *pc* (the program counter) which indicates which step of the protocol the thread is currently in, and  
   * *value* (a numeric field) that the thread uses to remember a snapshot of a shared counter.

2. **Shared counter** – a single natural‑number variable that all threads can read and later update.

At the start of execution every thread is in the “Read” phase, its *value* field is zero, and the shared counter is also zero.

---

**Thread Actions**

The system evolves by repeatedly letting any thread perform one of the following actions, or by entering a global “terminating” state once every thread has finished.

| Action | When it can be taken | Effect on the thread’s local state | Effect on the shared counter |
|--------|----------------------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------|
| **Read** | The thread’s *pc* is “Read”. | The thread changes its *pc* to “Inc” and copies the current value of the shared counter into its *value* field. | The shared counter is left unchanged. |
| **Inc** | The thread’s *pc* is “Inc”. | The thread changes its *pc* to “Done”. | The shared counter is updated to the value that the thread stored in its *value* field plus one. |
| **Terminating** | All threads have *pc* equal to “Done”. | No thread state is changed. | The shared counter is left unchanged; the system simply stops making further moves. |

In other words, each thread follows a two‑step protocol:

1. **Read phase** – grab a snapshot of the current counter.  
2. **Increment phase** – write back a new counter value that is exactly one larger than the snapshot it read.

A thread may not skip either step, and it may not perform the increment before it has performed the read. The two steps can be interleaved arbitrarily among the threads: for example, *t1* may read, then *t2* may read, then *t1* may increment, then *t2* may increment, etc.

---

**Safety Goal (Invariant)**

The invariant that the model‑checker verifies is called **NoLostUpdates**. It asserts that **once every thread has reached the “Done” state, the shared counter must equal the total number of threads**. In the concrete instance with two threads, the invariant guarantees that after both threads have completed their two‑step protocol the counter will be exactly 2. The invariant therefore ensures that no increment performed by a thread can be lost or overwritten by another thread’s later actions.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
If all threads have finished their protocol (each is in the “Done” state), then the shared counter’s value equals the number of threads, meaning that every thread’s increment has been correctly applied and no update has been lost.

**System Overview**

The model describes a set of concurrent threads (named *processes*) that coordinate access to a single critical section by using a futex‑style lock.  
Each thread repeatedly executes a three‑phase loop:

1. **Attempt to acquire the lock** (`lock_mutex`).  
2. **Execute the critical section** (represented by a no‑op placeholder).  
3. **Release the lock** (`unlock_mutex`).

All threads share two global data structures:

* **Lock state (`futex_state`)** – an integer that can hold the values 0, 1, or 2.  
  * 0 means the lock is free.  
  * 1 means a thread has just taken the lock without finding any contention.  
  * 2 means the lock is held and at least one other thread is waiting.

* **Sleep set (`futex_sleepers`)** – the set of thread identifiers that are currently blocked waiting for the lock to become available.

Each thread also maintains a small amount of private data:

* **Program counter (`pc`)** – indicates which step of the algorithm the thread is currently executing (e.g., “Loop”, “ExchangeLock”, “Check”, “SleepLoop”, “SleepCheck”, “WaitForWake”, “CS”, “ExchangeUnlock”, etc.).
* **Local copy of the expected value (`val`)** – used by the `futex_wait` routine to remember the value that the thread expects the lock to have before it goes to sleep.
* **Local copy of the previous lock state (`old_state_` for lock, `old_state` for unlock)** – used to decide whether the thread must sleep or must wake another thread.
* **Call stack (`stack`)** – a per‑thread stack that records pending return points when a procedure calls another procedure (for example, when `lock_mutex` calls `futex_wait`). The stack is purely a bookkeeping device for the model and does not affect the logical behavior of the lock.

---

### Detailed Actions

#### 1. `futex_wait(expected)`
* The thread reads the current lock state.  
* If the state differs from the value it expected, the routine returns immediately (the lock has already changed, so sleeping is unnecessary).  
* If the state matches the expected value, the thread adds itself to the global sleep set and then blocks.  
* The thread remains blocked until it is removed from the sleep set by a wake operation; at that point it returns to its caller.

#### 2. `futex_wake_all`
* Clears the entire sleep set, thereby waking **every** thread that is currently blocked in `futex_wait`.

#### 3. `futex_wake_single`
* If the sleep set is empty, the routine does nothing.  
* Otherwise it selects **one** thread from the sleep set (the model does not prescribe which) and removes that thread from the set, waking it.

#### 4. `lock_mutex`
* **Fast path (exchange)** – The thread records the current lock state in `old_state_` and then writes the value 1 into `futex_state`.  
  * If the recorded old state was 0, the lock was free; the thread proceeds immediately to the critical section.  
  * If the old state was not 0, the thread knows there is contention and enters the slow path.

* **Slow path (contention handling)** – The thread enters a loop that repeats the following steps until it acquires the lock:  
  1. Record the current lock state in `old_state_`.  
  2. Write the value 2 into `futex_state` to indicate “locked and contested”.  
  3. If the recorded old state was 0, the lock has become free and the thread exits the loop, proceeding to the critical section.  
  4. Otherwise the thread calls `futex_wait(2)`, which will block the thread (adding it to the sleep set) until another thread wakes it.

#### 5. `unlock_mutex`
* The thread records the current lock state in `old_state` and then writes 0 into `futex_state`, thereby releasing the lock.  
* If the recorded old state was 2, the releasing thread knows that at least one other thread is waiting; it therefore invokes `futex_wake_single` to wake exactly one waiting thread.  
* If the recorded old state was not 2, no thread is waiting, so the unlock operation simply returns.

#### 6. Thread Main Loop (`p`)
* **Loop** – The thread pushes a call to `lock_mutex` onto its stack, resets its local `old_state_` to 0, and jumps to the `ExchangeLock` step of `lock_mutex`.  
* **Critical Section (`CS`)** – After a successful lock acquisition, the thread executes the critical section (a placeholder `skip`). It then pushes a call to `unlock_mutex` onto its stack and jumps to the `ExchangeUnlock` step of `unlock_mutex`.  
* The thread repeats this loop forever.

---

### Intended Behaviour

* Only one thread may be inside the critical section at any moment.  
* If a thread finds the lock already taken, it will eventually be placed in the sleep set and later be woken by the thread that releases the lock.  
* The lock can be released either by a thread that acquired it without contention (fast path) or by a thread that acquired it after having waited (slow path).  
* The wake‑up policy is *fair* in the sense that the model includes weak fairness assumptions for every enabled action, guaranteeing that a thread that continually remains enabled will eventually make progress.

---

### Safety Property

The invariant asserted in the model guarantees **mutual exclusion**: no two distinct threads can be in the critical section at the same time.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** At any reachable state, it is never the case that two different threads are simultaneously executing the critical section. In other words, for every pair of distinct threads, at most one of them can be in the critical-section state at any moment.

**System Overview** The model describes a small multi‑transaction database engine that supports a fixed number of concurrent transactions. Each transaction performs a sequence of read and write operations on a set of versioned values, then either commits or rolls back. The engine enforces snapshot‑style isolation: a transaction sees only those value versions that were committed before it started, plus any versions it itself creates. Conflicting writes cause the later transaction to be aborted. **State Variables** | Variable | Meaning | |----------|---------| | **next_transaction_id** | A monotonically increasing counter that supplies a unique identifier to each transaction when it begins. | | **transactions** | A table (indexed by transaction numbers) that holds, for every transaction, the following fields:
• **pc** – the current phase of the transaction (`Begin`, `ReadWrite`, `Complete`, or `Done`).
• **ops** – the number of read or write operations already performed.
• **id** – the unique transaction identifier assigned at start (or a special null value before start).
• **state** – the final status of the transaction (`InProgress`, `Committed`, or `RolledBack`).
• **active_set** – the set of other transactions that were active when this transaction started.
• **read_set** – an ordered list of the value versions that the transaction has read.
• **write_set** – the set of value versions that the transaction has written (or attempted to write). | | **active_transactions** | The set of transaction indices that are currently executing (i.e., whose `pc` is not `Done`). | | **values** | A chronological list of all value versions that have ever existed. Each entry records:
• **id** – a logical key identifying the logical data item (the position in the list, i.e., the version number).
• **start_tx_id** – the identifier of the transaction that created this version.
• **end_tx_id** – the identifier of the transaction that later superseded this version, or a special null value if the version is still the latest. | **Transaction Lifecycle Actions** 1. **Begin (TxBegin)** *Precondition*: The transaction is in the `Begin` phase. *Effect*: The engine assigns the next free transaction identifier to the transaction, records the current set of active transactions as the transaction’s `active_set`, changes its state to `InProgress`, moves its phase to `ReadWrite`, increments the global transaction‑id counter, and adds the transaction to the `active_transactions` set. No values are changed. 2. **Read (TxRead)** *Precondition*: The transaction is in the `ReadWrite` phase. *Effect*: If the transaction has already performed the maximum allowed number of operations (`MaxOps`), it moves to the `Complete` phase without reading. Otherwise the transaction selects a value version that is **visible** to it (see visibility rule below), appends that version to its `read_set`, increments its operation count, and leaves the global value list unchanged. The transaction stays in the `ReadWrite` phase. 3. **Write (TxWrite)** *Precondition*: The transaction is in the `ReadWrite` phase. *Effect*: If the transaction has already reached `MaxOps`, it moves to `Complete` without writing. Otherwise two possibilities exist: *a) Create a brand‑new version*: a fresh entry is appended to the global `values` list with a new logical key, the current transaction’s identifier as `start_tx_id`, and `end_tx_id` set to null. The transaction’s operation counter is increased. *b) Update an existing visible version*: the transaction first picks a visible version, then creates a new version that either (i) re‑starts the version with its own `start_tx_id` (overwrites) or (ii) marks the old version as superseded by setting its `end_tx_id` to the current transaction’s identifier. In both sub‑cases a new entry is appended to `values`, the transaction’s `write_set` is updated to include the original version it touched, and the operation counter is increased. No other state is changed. 4. **Complete (TxComplete)** *Precondition*: The transaction is in the `Complete` phase. *Effect*: The transaction attempts to finalize. It either (i) rolls back unconditionally, or (ii) evaluates whether a conflict exists (see conflict rule below). If a conflict is detected, the transaction rolls back; otherwise it commits. In either case the transaction’s phase becomes `Done`, its final state is recorded (`RolledBack` or `Committed`), and it is removed from the `active_transactions` set. The list of values is left unchanged. 5. **Termination** The system is considered to have reached a stable end state when every transaction has reached the `Done` phase and has performed exactly `MaxOps` operations. At that point the whole state stops evolving. **Visibility Rule (ValuesVisibleForTx)** A value version is visible to a transaction **T** if all of the following hold: * The version’s `end_tx_id` is still null (i.e., it has not been superseded). * Either the version was created by a transaction that committed before **T** started and that earlier transaction is **not** in **T**’s `active_set`, or the version was created by **T** itself. Among all visible versions that share the same logical key, the transaction sees only the **latest** one (the one with the greatest `start_tx_id`). The set of those latest visible versions is what a read operation may choose from. **Conflict Detection (HasConflict)** A transaction **T** is said to have a conflict if any of the following holds: * Some transaction that was already active when **T** started later committed and wrote to at least one logical key that **T** also intends to write. * Some transaction that started after **T** (i.e., with a larger identifier) later committed and wrote to at least one logical key that **T** also intends to write. If any such overlapping write sets are found, **T** must abort during the `Complete` step. **Safety Guarantees (the invariant)** The model checks five safety properties simultaneously: 1. **No dirty reads** – Every value a transaction reads either belongs to that transaction itself or, if it belongs to another transaction, that other transaction must have committed. 2. **Repeatable read** – If a transaction reads two versions of the same logical key, either the two reads return the identical version or the later read sees a version that was created by the transaction itself. 3. **Only reads from snapshot** – For any two reads of the same logical key performed by a transaction, the `start_tx_id` of the earlier read is never larger than that of the later read; the transaction never observes a newer committed version after it has already seen an older one. 4. **Conflicting writes abort transaction** – Whenever a transaction commits, any other transaction that was still active at the time of the commit and that wrote to any of the same logical keys must be forced to roll back. 5. **Every transaction completes** – When a transaction reaches the `Done` phase, its final state is always either `Committed` or `RolledBack`; no transaction remains in an indeterminate state. These properties together ensure that the system provides snapshot isolation with automatic abort of write‑conflicts, and that all transactions eventually finish with a well‑defined outcome. **SAFETY PROPERTY:** The system guarantees that every transaction sees a consistent snapshot of the database (no dirty or non‑repeatable reads), reads only values that were committed before the transaction started or that it created itself, never observes a newer version after seeing an older one, aborts any transaction that conflicts on writes with a transaction that later commits, and finally leaves each transaction in a definitive state of either committed or rolled back.

**System Overview**

The model describes a small railway yard that contains two trains ( Train 1 and Train 2 ), a pair of track sections, two switches, and four signal lights.  

* **Train positions** – `t1` records where Train 1 is, and `t2` records where Train 2 is. Each variable can hold one of the named locations:  
  * “TRACK1”, “TRACK2”, “TRACK3”, “TRACK4” – the four straight track segments.  
  * “SWITCH1”, “SWITCH2” – the two junction points (the physical location of each switch).  

* **Signal lights** – `s1` through `s4` are the four signals that guard entry onto the four track‑segment‑to‑switch connections:  
  * `s1` protects the movement from TRACK1 onto SWITCH1.  
  * `s2` protects the movement from TRACK2 onto SWITCH2.  
  * `s3` protects the movement from TRACK3 onto SWITCH1.  
  * `s4` protects the movement from TRACK4 onto SWITCH2.  

  Each signal can be either **STOP** (red) or **GO** (green).

* **Switch settings** – `sw1` and `sw2` describe the physical alignment of the two switches:  
  * `sw1` can be **STRAIGHT** (the default, connecting TRACK1 ↔ SWITCH1 ↔ TRACK2) or **LEFT** (connecting TRACK1 ↔ SWITCH1 ↔ TRACK3).  
  * `sw2` can be **STRAIGHT** (connecting TRACK4 ↔ SWITCH2 ↔ TRACK2) or **RIGHT** (connecting TRACK4 ↔ SWITCH2 ↔ TRACK3).  

All variables are required to stay within these admissible sets (the *type‑checking* part of the invariant).

---

### Actions (State Transitions)

1. **MoveT1 – Train 1 advances**  
   *If Train 1 is at a location that has a green signal, it may move forward to the next location, and the signal it just passed is set back to STOP.*  
   The possible steps are:  
   - From TRACK1 to SWITCH1 (requires `s1 = GO`). After the move `s1` becomes STOP.  
   - From SWITCH1 to TRACK2 (no signal needed).  
   - From TRACK2 to SWITCH2 (requires `s2 = GO`). After the move `s2` becomes STOP.  
   - From SWITCH2 to TRACK4 (no signal needed).  

   All other variables (Train 2, all signals, and both switches) stay unchanged.

2. **MoveT2 – Train 2 advances**  
   *Analogous to MoveT1, but traveling the opposite direction and using the second switch.*  
   The possible steps are:  
   - From TRACK4 to SWITCH2 (requires `s4 = GO`). After the move `s4` becomes STOP.  
   - From SWITCH2 to the next track, which depends on the current setting of `sw2`:  
     * If `sw2 = STRAIGHT` the train goes to TRACK2.  
     * If `sw2 = RIGHT` the train goes to TRACK3.  
   - From TRACK3 to SWITCH1 (requires `s3 = GO`). After the move `s3` becomes STOP.  
   - From SWITCH1 to TRACK1 (no signal needed).  

   All other variables (Train 1, all signals, and both switches) stay unchanged.

3. **ChangeS1 – Set signal 1 to GO**  
   This action turns the red signal at the entrance of SWITCH1 (signal 1) green when the following conditions hold:  
   - Train 1 is still at TRACK1 (has not yet entered the switch).  
   - Train 2 is not occupying TRACK2 or SWITCH1 (so the route is clear).  
   - Switch 1 is currently in the STRAIGHT position (so the intended path is TRACK1 → SWITCH1 → TRACK2).  

   Only `s1` changes; everything else stays the same.

4. **ChangeS2 – Set signal 2 to GO**  
   Turns signal 2 green when:  
   - Train 1 is at TRACK2.  
   - Train 2 is not on TRACK4 or SWITCH2 (the opposite direction is clear).  
   - Switch 2 is currently in the STRAIGHT position (so the intended path is TRACK2 → SWITCH2 → TRACK4).  

   Only `s2` changes.

5. **ChangeS3 – Set signal 3 to GO**  
   Turns signal 3 green when:  
   - Train 2 is at TRACK3.  
   - Train 1 is not on TRACK1 or SWITCH1 (so the opposite direction is clear).  
   - Switch 1 is set to LEFT (so the path from TRACK3 via SWITCH1 leads toward TRACK1).  

   Only `s3` changes.

6. **ChangeS4 – Set signal 4 to GO**  
   Turns signal 4 green when:  
   - Train 2 is at TRACK4.  
   - Train 1 is not on TRACK3 or SWITCH2 (the opposite direction is clear).  
   - Switch 2 is set to RIGHT (so the path from TRACK4 via SWITCH2 leads toward TRACK3).  

   Only `s4` changes.

7. **ChangeSw1 – Flip Switch 1**  
   The switch can be toggled only when no train is occupying SWITCH1 and both signals that protect that junction (`s1` and `s3`) are STOP. Two possibilities:  
   - If the switch is currently STRAIGHT and Train 2 is on TRACK3 (meaning the left‑hand route is needed), the switch is turned to LEFT.  
   - If the switch is currently LEFT and Train 1 is on TRACK1 (meaning the straight route is needed), the switch is turned back to STRAIGHT.  

   No train positions or signal values are altered.

8. **ChangeSw2 – Flip Switch 2**  
   Similar to ChangeSw1, but for the second junction. The switch can change only when no train is on SWITCH2 and both signals `s2` and `s4` are STOP. Two possibilities:  
   - If the switch is STRAIGHT and Train 2 is on TRACK4, it is turned to RIGHT (to allow a train coming from TRACK4 to head toward TRACK3).  
   - If the switch is RIGHT and Train 1 is on TRACK2 (meaning the straight route is needed again), the switch is turned back to STRAIGHT.  

   Again, only the switch variable changes.

All actions are combined in the **Next** relation, meaning that at each step the system may perform any one of the eight actions that is currently enabled.

**Fairness** constraints are declared for each action, guaranteeing that if an action remains continuously enabled it will eventually be taken. This prevents the model from stalling forever on a particular enabled move.

---

### Intended Behaviour

Initially, both trains are at opposite ends of the yard (Train 1 on TRACK1, Train 2 on TRACK4) with all signals at STOP and both switches aligned straight. The system repeatedly:

1. Turns the appropriate signal green when the track ahead is clear and the switch is in the correct position.  
2. Moves the train forward when its signal is green.  
3. Adjusts the switches when both directions are idle and the upcoming traffic requires a different routing.

Through this coordinated sequence the two trains can pass each other safely: Train 1 proceeds from TRACK1 → SWITCH1 → TRACK2 → SWITCH2 → TRACK4, while Train 2 proceeds from TRACK4 → SWITCH2 → TRACK3 → SWITCH1 → TRACK1. The model checks that this crossing can eventually complete without the two trains ever occupying the same location.

---

### Invariants (Safety Conditions)

The configuration file asks the model checker to maintain two invariants throughout every possible execution:

* **TypeOk** – All variables always hold values from their declared domains (positions, signal colours, and switch settings).  
* **TrainsNeverCollide** – At no time do the two trains share the same location.

These invariants are proved to hold for all reachable states under the fairness assumptions.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The system guarantees that the two trains are never on the same track segment or switch at the same time; i.e., the positions of Train 1 and Train 2 are always different, ensuring that a collision can never occur.

**System Overview**

The model describes a very simple two‑component state machine that passes a piece of data together with a binary “toggle” flag between two logical agents, called **A** and **B**.

* **Data domain** – The only possible data values are the elements of the constant set `Data`. In the concrete model this set is `{a, b}`.

* **State variables** –  
  * **AVar** – a pair `(d, f)` where `d` is a value taken from `Data` and `f` is a flag that can be either `0` or `1`.  
  * **BVar** – another pair `(d, f)` of the same shape.  

  Both variables are always required to contain a data value together with a flag; this is enforced by the `TypeOk` condition.

* **Initial state** – At the start, the flag of `AVar` is `1` and `BVar` is exactly the same pair as `AVar`. Thus the system begins with both agents holding an identical data‑flag pair, the flag being `1`.

* **Actions** – The system evolves by repeatedly executing one of two actions, **A** or **B**.

  * **Action A (the “producer” step)**  
    * It may fire only when the two variables are currently equal (`AVar = BVar`).  
    * It chooses a new data element `d` (any element of `Data`).  
    * It updates **AVar** to the pair `(d, 1‑f)`, where `f` is the flag that AVar previously held; in other words, the flag is flipped from `0` to `1` or from `1` to `0`.  
    * **BVar** remains unchanged.  
    * The effect is that the producer creates a fresh data value and toggles its own flag while leaving the consumer’s copy untouched.

  * **Action B (the “consumer” step)**  
    * It may fire only when the two variables differ (`AVar ≠ BVar`).  
    * It copies the entire content of **AVar** into **BVar**, making the two variables equal again.  
    * **AVar** stays unchanged.  
    * This step represents the consumer receiving the latest data‑flag pair from the producer.

* **Execution policy** – The specification requires that the system always be able to take a step (`[][Next]_vars`) and that the **B** action is *weakly fair*: if B becomes continuously enabled, it must eventually be taken. In practice this guarantees that whenever A produces a new pair, B will eventually copy it.

* **Liveness guarantee** – The property `BEventuallyReceives` states that for every possible pair `(d, f)` that ever appears in **AVar**, the system will eventually bring **BVar** to that same pair. In other words, any value produced by A is eventually observed by B.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
If the flags of the two agents are equal, then the entire pairs must be identical; i.e., the system never allows a situation where AVar and BVar have the same flag but different data values. This invariant ensures that the only way the flags can match is when the two agents are perfectly synchronized on both data and flag.
